name: Almería
title: Almería Ship Gauging: UTM for Ferries and Bulk Carriers
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Almería for North Africa ro-pax ferries, bulk carriers and general cargo ships: hull, hold and tank gauging.
h1: Thickness Gauging in Almería: Hull Surveys for Ferries and Bulk Ships
intro: Almería lies on the south-east corner of Spain, closer to the Algerian and Moroccan coasts than to most Spanish cities, and its port reflects that with regular ferries to Melilla, Nador and Ghazaouet alongside bulk and general cargo. Ships spend predictable hours alongside, which suits planned gauging. Our ultrasonic thickness technicians fly in from India to meet the vessel, with the ship's agent arranging access, and the work is focused on holds, ballast tanks, decks, ramps and piping.

highlights.p: Ro-pax ships crossing to Melilla, Nador and Ghazaouet carry heavy vehicle traffic. Car decks, ramps and ballast tanks wear in service, and a measured set of readings tells the technical manager where steel is thinning before the overhaul.

highlights.h: Hold and coaming gauging on bulkers
highlights.p: Bulk carriers loading or discharging in Almería have holds that empty between cargoes. That is the moment to read frames, hopper plating and hatch coamings, while the compartments are clean and the crew can organise safe access.

There is no large drydock in Almería, so owners dock their ships in Cartagena, Cádiz or Gibraltar. Gauging here gives the yard and the superintendent a measured steel estimate in advance of the docking quotation.

port.h: The port of Almería: ferries, marble, gypsum and cement
p: The Autoridad Portuaria de Almería manages a harbour set beneath the Alcazaba on a wide bay open to the south, with the western breakwater giving shelter from the dominant seas. The approach is simple and the pilots board outside the entrance, though a strong levante wind can complicate berthing and sometimes holds ships offshore. The commercial quays lie to the east of the passenger terminal, with the fishing harbour in a separate basin, so the traffic flows are well separated and each ship type has its own berths.

Passenger traffic is built around the African link. Ferries sail to Melilla and to the Moroccan port of Nador, and others run to Ghazaouet on the Algerian coast, with peaks in summer when returning residents travel with their vehicles. The cargo side is typical of south-east Spain: marble from the Macael quarries and other building stone, gypsum, cement and clinker, fertiliser and agricultural inputs, plus general cargo in coasters. Smaller tankers and bunker barges serve the port, and tugs and fishing boats share the basins. Occasional cruise calls and visits from naval ships add some variety to a mostly working harbour.

Seasonality is clear. Ferry traffic swells from late spring to the end of summer and then falls, leaving winter as the practical period for maintenance. Bulk ships keep a steadier rhythm, though loading windows depend on quarry output and on weather, and delays at berth are common when levante is strong. Because the tide range is small, draught is set by the quay depth and not by the water level. The anchorage in the bay is used by ships waiting for a berth, and some coasters wait there for cargo orders, which can leave a vessel idle for a day or more.

Gauging in Almería is nearly always done alongside. Passenger ferries sit at the passenger terminal between rotations, with their ramps lowered and car decks empty, and that is the most convenient time to read ramp plating, deck structure and the tank tops below. Bulk ships at the commercial quays discharge or load and then wait for documents, and during those gaps the cleaned holds can be opened for frame, bulkhead and coaming readings, provided the loading plan allows it and the terminal permits entry.

There is no drydock in the port for deep-sea tonnage. Smaller harbour craft and fishing boats are looked after by local workshops and slipways, but ships of any size that need steel renewal go elsewhere, usually to Cartagena, the Bay of Cádiz or Gibraltar. For these ships the Almería stop is the time to build a measured picture of the structure, so the owner knows what to expect before approaching a yard. Gauging ships at anchor is only realistic for short checks, and depends on launch access and sea state.
list: Passenger terminal berths for the African ferries — ramp, car-deck, ballast tank and piping gauging between rotations
Commercial quays handling stone, gypsum and cement — hold frame, hopper, coaming and deck readings on bulk carriers once holds are clean
General cargo berths — hull, tween deck and hatch cover gauging on coasters during short cargo stops
Bunkering and tanker berths — deck, pump room and ballast tank readings on small product tankers, under terminal permit rules
Almería Bay anchorage — short sampling jobs on ships waiting for cargo orders, subject to sea state and launch access
Nearest drydocks at Cartagena, Cádiz and Gibraltar — gauging started here can be completed beside the docking survey

context.h: Port state control and the trades around Almería
p: Port state control at Almería falls under the Paris MoU and is carried out by Spain's Capitanía Marítima, part of the Dirección General de la Marina Mercante. Inspectors give particular attention to ships on older tonnage and to ferries working busy short routes, and their questions often come back to structural wastage, hatch cover condition and the state of ballast and fire-fighting piping. Measured thickness readings are the answer when a master has to show that steel is within limits.

Several EU rules shape owner decisions. The Ship Recycling Regulation asks ships calling at EU ports to carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials, EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime put a cost of carbon on voyages into and out of Spain, and old tonnage trading to Africa is under steady pressure to justify its steel. The Almería hinterland produces stone, horticultural goods and minerals, and the port's bulk and ro-ro business grows or shrinks with them. A ship on a frequent North Africa rotation can accumulate wear quickly in its ramps and decks, and regular gauging between dockings keeps surprises away from the survey.

jobs.h: Gauging jobs we see at Almería
jobs.p: The work in Almería follows two patterns: short, repeated visits to ferries on fixed rotations, and thorough surveys of bulk and general cargo ships that stay alongside for a few days. Scope, access arrangements and the report format are agreed with the superintendent before the technicians travel, so that time alongside is spent measuring. Typical jobs include:
list: Ramp, car-deck and ballast tank gauging on an African route ferry ahead of its winter overhaul.
Hold frame, hopper plating and hatch coaming readings on a bulk carrier after discharging gypsum or cement.
Pre-docking steel estimate for a coaster, taking deck, shell and tank top readings before it heads to a yard in Cartagena or Cádiz.
Scrubber and sea-water piping gauging on a ro-pax ship, compared with earlier readings to establish a corrosion rate.
On-hire or off-hire condition gauging on a general cargo ship changing charterer in southern Spain.

logistics: The nearest international airport is Almería, with seasonal links to European cities; most technicians from India fly via Madrid or another European hub and reach the port by road or a domestic flight. Málaga and Alicante airports are alternatives with wider connections. The ship's agent arranges port passes and a launch for any anchorage job. Schengen visas are required, so please send the vessel's dates as early as possible; once visas are issued we confirm the mobilisation against the ship's schedule.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged while a bulk carrier is at the Almería quay?
faqs.a: Often, once a hold has been discharged and cleaned. Frames, hopper plating, bulkheads and hatch coamings can be read if the loading plan leaves the hold empty long enough and the terminal allows entry. Work stops when cargo operations resume, so the hold sequence is agreed with the agent and the chief officer in advance.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Almería?
faqs.a: No dock for deep-sea ships. Small craft are handled by local slipways, but ferries, bulkers and coasters needing steel renewal usually go to Cartagena, the Bay of Cádiz or Gibraltar. Gauging in Almería gives you measured wastage figures to take to the yard, and helps compare quotations on a common basis.

faqs.q: How do North Africa ferries fit around gauging?
faqs.a: They can be gauged between rotations if the crew prepares the ramp and car deck spaces and the tank access in advance. Summer is the peak period and the ship may have little spare time, so winter overhauls are the better moment for programmes that need gas-freeing, staging or several days alongside.

faqs.q: Can a ship at anchor in Almería Bay be gauged?
faqs.a: Short jobs are possible when a launch can be arranged and the sea state allows. A ship waiting for cargo orders may be idle, but weather and the berth schedule can change quickly, so a narrow list of spaces is more realistic than a full survey. If the stay is long, a berth is normally preferable.

faqs.q: What does the report look like?
faqs.a: It follows the usual layout for thickness measurement reports, with plan sketches, gauged items, original and measured thickness and a note of the readings that fall near allowable limits. The superintendent can use it for steel estimates and discussions with class; whether it counts for credit to a survey is explained in the class section on this page.
